**Chapter I**

**INTRODUCTION**

Information and Communications Technology (ICT) has become an important component of modern transportation systems, particularly through the development of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). These systems integrate computational technologies, communication networks, sensing technologies, and transportation data to support traffic monitoring, incident management, mobility, and transportation safety. Research on ITS has identified its potential to improve urban mobility and traffic management while also recognizing challenges associated with the implementation and integration of intelligent transportation technologies (Waqar et al., 2023). Similarly, advances in computer vision and other computational techniques have expanded the capabilities of ITS in areas such as traffic monitoring, incident detection, road-condition assessment, and transportation safety (Dilek & Dener, 2023). These developments have contributed to the evolution of navigation applications from conventional digital mapping tools toward systems capable of incorporating dynamic transportation information into route-planning decisions.  
The increasing availability of location-based and crowdsourced transportation data has further expanded the amount of information that can be used to monitor road conditions. Crowdsourced traffic information can complement conventional traffic-monitoring sources by providing incident information from road users themselves. For example, Amin-Naseri et al. (2018) found that crowdsourced incident reports from Waze provided additional coverage and timely information that could complement existing traffic-management data. More recent research likewise found that Waze event reports can provide useful information concerning traffic incidents, although their coverage, timeliness, and spatial accuracy vary across locations and over time (Liu et al., 2023). These findings demonstrate both the value of community-generated transportation information and the importance of evaluating its quality before it is used to support transportation decisions.  
The issue becomes more significant when a road incident affects road passability rather than merely traffic speed. A road may experience reduced accessibility or become completely unavailable because of flooding, fallen trees, debris, construction activities, vehicular collisions, or temporary road closures. In these circumstances, determining whether a road can still be traversed may be more important than estimating the amount of traffic on that road. Research on safe route-finding has emphasized the importance of incorporating real-time traffic and incident information into navigation and route-selection processes, while also identifying challenges in developing routing approaches that account for dynamic safety conditions (Sohrabi et al., 2022). Studies focusing specifically on flooding have similarly demonstrated that flood events can alter road accessibility and network functionality, making information about affected road segments relevant to both mobility and emergency decision-making (Alabbad et al., 2024; Panakkal et al., 2023).  
The dynamic nature of road hazards also creates a challenge for information systems. Conditions on an affected road can change over relatively short periods, while information collected through different sources may vary in accuracy, location, and timeliness. In the context of flooding, for example, researchers have noted that rapidly changing conditions can make real-time assessment of road impacts difficult, while crowdsourced and other data sources can provide additional information for monitoring affected transportation networks (Kong et al., 2022; Panakkal et al., 2023). This suggests that a navigation system intended to support decisions during road disruptions must consider not only the availability of hazard information but also whether that information accurately represents the current condition of the affected road.  
Crowdsourcing provides an opportunity to obtain information from road users who may directly observe incidents that are not immediately available through conventional monitoring systems. However, crowdsourced information also presents data-quality challenges. Reports may differ in reliability because of variations in user participation, geographic coverage, reporting behavior, and the accuracy of individual observations. Liu et al. (2023) specifically examined the coverage, timeliness, and location accuracy of Waze reports and demonstrated that the characteristics of crowdsourced incident data can vary over time. Similarly, research on crowdsourced transportation data has identified the need to evaluate its reliability and coverage when used as a complement to conventional traffic information (Amin-Naseri et al., 2018). Therefore, the usefulness of a collaborative road-hazard information system depends not only on encouraging users to submit reports but also on establishing mechanisms for assessing the credibility and validity of those reports.  
The need for reliable hazard information extends beyond individual commuters. Road accessibility is also relevant to emergency response and other transportation-related decision-making activities. During flooding and other disruptive events, inaccessible road segments can affect the ability of emergency personnel and the public to reach destinations and critical facilities. Alabbad et al. (2024), for instance, demonstrated the use of a web-based decision-support framework to analyze flood impacts on road accessibility and support routing and emergency-planning decisions. Research on road passability during flood events has likewise emphasized the importance of determining whether roads remain accessible to support situational awareness and emergency operations (Lopez-Fuentes et al., 2020). These findings indicate that information concerning road-blocking hazards may have practical value for multiple stakeholders, provided that the information is sufficiently timely and reliable.  
Another consideration is the relationship between automated assessment and human judgment. Automated mechanisms can assist in processing large amounts of user-generated information, but uncertainty in human-generated data remains an important concern. Research on trustworthy human computation emphasizes that systems involving human-generated information require mechanisms for establishing and maintaining trust between users and computational processes (Kashima et al., 2024). In a road-hazard reporting context, this suggests that user reputation or automated assessment alone may not be sufficient for resolving every report. Reports that conflict with other observations, contain insufficient evidence, or exhibit characteristics associated with unreliable information may require additional validation before being treated as authoritative.  
Despite the development of intelligent transportation systems, crowdsourced navigation, and dynamic route-planning technologies, a need remains for navigation approaches that specifically consider road passability and the reliability of road-blocking hazard information. Existing research demonstrates that crowdsourced transportation data can supplement conventional monitoring systems, but it also shows that the quality, coverage, and accuracy of such information require evaluation (Amin-Naseri et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2023). At the same time, studies on safe routing and flood-related transportation disruptions demonstrate the importance of incorporating dynamic road conditions into route-planning and accessibility decisions (Sohrabi et al., 2022; Alabbad et al., 2024). Taken together, these findings point to a research gap concerning the integration of community-generated hazard reports, information verification, road-passability assessment, and dynamic navigation support within a single system.  
Therefore, the problem addressed by this study is the lack of a dedicated navigation approach that can support the timely identification, reporting, verification, and communication of road-blocking hazards whose occurrence may cause roads to become partially or completely impassable.

**Objectives of the Project**

This study aims to design and develop RouteGuard, a collaborative navigation system for reporting, verifying, and communicating road-blocking hazards and providing alternative routes to support safer and more efficient urban travel. Specifically, the study seeks to:  
**SO1.** Develop and test a mobile application that enables users to submit categorized road-blocking hazard reports, identify reported hazards within a 5-kilometer proximity range, view confirmed hazards, and receive location-based notifications at least 500 meters before reaching an eligible confirmed, route-relevant hazard during system testing.

**SO2.** Implement and evaluate a dynamic route-planning module that generates an alternative route when a confirmed hazard affects the user’s planned route, achieving a target route-recalculation response time of no more than 3 seconds under the defined test environment.

**SO3.** Implement and evaluate a hazard-report credibility mechanism comprising a user reputation score, based on a reporting user’s historical reporting accuracy, and a report-confidence score, based on report age, confirmations, denials, and contributor reputation; the mechanism is designed to inform report credibility and moderation priority rather than to independently confirm reports, with final confirmation remaining the responsibility of human moderation, and with the mechanism’s effectiveness assessed using classification accuracy and false-positive measurements during system testing.

**SO4.** Develop and evaluate a web-based MIO administrative dashboard that enables authorized personnel to create, update, and remove official road advisories, with advisory updates reflected in the mobile application within a target propagation time of no more than 5 seconds under the defined test environment.

**SO5.** Implement and evaluate a moderation module that enables authorized moderators to review flagged hazard reports and classify them as confirmed, false, or inconclusive, with moderation decisions automatically updating the corresponding user’s reputation score and the module’s functionality verified through predefined test cases.

**Scope and Delimitations of the Project**

The project encompasses the design and development of RouteGuard, an Android-based collaborative navigation application intended to support the reporting, credibility assessment, moderation, and communication of road-blocking hazards. The mobile application includes a map interface for viewing active hazard reports, location-based notifications, categorized user reporting, hazard visualization, and alternative route visualization. It also includes a prototype responder view for demonstration of how confirmed and active road-hazard reports could be presented to rescue and emergency personnel; this prototype is not integrated with an actual response agency. In addition, the project includes a web-based administrative dashboard with two authorized roles: Municipal Information Office (MIO) personnel, who can create, update, and remove official road advisories, and System Moderators, who can review flagged user-submitted reports and classify them as confirmed, false, or inconclusive. The system backend uses Node.js for server-side application services, PostgreSQL for persistent data storage, Valkey for caching and related high-speed data operations, OpenStreetMap for map and road-network data, and a self-hosted Open Source Routing Machine (OSRM) instance for route computation. The routing component uses OSRM's Multi-Level Dijkstra (MLD) algorithm to support efficient route recalculation when confirmed road hazards affect the accessibility of road segments. The project covers the integration of these components to support user-generated hazard reporting, report-confidence assessment and human moderation, official advisories, hazard notification, and dynamic route planning within the selected study area.  
The project is delimited to Tacloban City, Leyte, which serves as the testing environment; therefore, the results may not represent road conditions, transportation patterns, or user behavior in other geographic areas. The mobile application is limited to the Android platform, while iOS and other mobile operating systems are excluded from the current development scope. The web-based administrative dashboard, including the MIO and moderation modules, is developed as a prototype and is not integrated with the existing information systems, databases, or official records of an actual local government unit. Similarly, the responder view is intended for system demonstration and testing and does not establish an operational connection with any actual rescue, emergency response, or public safety agency. The system is limited to road-blocking hazards that affect road passability, such as flooding, fallen trees, accidents, debris, construction-related obstructions, and road closures; it does not function as a general-purpose disaster management, emergency broadcast, or public warning system. Hazard information is dependent on user-submitted reports and authorized official advisories; the system does not independently detect physical hazards through dedicated roadside sensors, satellite systems, or autonomous computer-vision mechanisms. Report credibility assessment is based on the implemented reputation and confidence mechanisms, while final report verification is performed through human moderation and does not attempt to automatically determine whether a report is fabricated, AI-generated, or intentionally misleading. Advanced predictive modeling, automated hazard forecasting, and artificial-intelligence-based prediction of future road obstructions are also excluded from the project. Finally, the prototype may rely on free-tier or publicly available third-party services and data sources, which may impose usage limits, coverage constraints, or service availability restrictions during development and testing.

**Significance of the Project**

The successful development of RouteGuard is expected to benefit the following stakeholders:

* Commuters and Other Road Users. RouteGuard can provide them with timely information about confirmed road-blocking hazards that may affect their planned routes. By presenting hazard locations, road-passability information, and alternative routes, the system can support more informed travel decisions and help users avoid roads that may be partially or completely impassable. The reporting function also provides road users with a structured means of sharing observed hazards with other users.

* Rescue and Emergency Response Teams. Authorized rescue and emergency response personnel may benefit from access to confirmed and active road-hazard information through the prototype responder view, which demonstrates future functionality and is not integrated with an actual response agency. Information about blocked or partially passable roads can support situational awareness and assist personnel in considering road accessibility when planning movement within an affected area. The system is intended to serve as an additional source of road-condition information and does not replace established emergency communication, dispatch, or response systems.

* Municipal Information Offices and Local Government Units. Municipal Information Offices (MIOs) may benefit from a dedicated channel for publishing official road advisories within the same platform used to communicate community-reported hazards. This can provide a means of distinguishing authorized municipal information from user-generated reports while allowing official information concerning roadworks, temporary closures, and other road conditions to reach system users. The collected and categorized community reports may also provide supplementary information regarding road conditions that may not be immediately available through official sources.

* System Moderators. They may benefit from a centralized mechanism for reviewing and resolving potentially unreliable or conflicting hazard reports. The moderation workflow provides a structured means of examining submitted reports, available supporting evidence, and reporter history before assigning a report a confirmed, false, or inconclusive status. The resulting moderation decisions can also contribute to the maintenance of user reputation records and the overall reliability of community-generated information within the system.

* Future Developers and Researchers. The project may serve as a reference for developing or extending collaborative navigation systems that integrate crowdsourced road-hazard reporting, information verification, official advisories, and dynamic route planning. The documented limitations of the prototype may also provide opportunities for future work involving broader geographic coverage, additional platforms, automated hazard detection, predictive modeling, and integration with official government or emergency-response systems.

**Chapter II**

**THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK**

**Theoretical Framework**

This study is anchored on two complementary theoretical perspectives that together explain why a crowdsourced, reputation-informed approach is an appropriate basis for a road-hazard navigation system: Trust and Reputation Theory in crowdsourced systems, and Collective Intelligence Theory as applied to crowdsourcing and citizen participation.  
Trust and Reputation Theory holds that, in systems where contributions come from many unverified individuals rather than a single accountable source, the system itself must generate mechanisms for estimating how much confidence to place in any given contribution, since the content of a report alone cannot establish its own reliability. Kashima, Oyama, Arai, and Mori (2024) frame this as a defining property of human computation: systems that depend on human-generated input require explicit mechanisms for establishing and maintaining trust between contributors and the platform, because uncertainty in human-generated data cannot be resolved by automated processing alone. Kanaparthy, Damle, and Gujar (2021) extend this idea temporally, proposing that a contributor's trustworthiness is best modeled not as a fixed label but as a score that rises gradually with sustained reliable behavior and falls sharply in response to unreliable behavior, so that the system rewards consistency while still responding quickly when a contributor's input becomes unreliable. Applied to RouteGuard, this theory directly grounds three design decisions: the assignment of a reputation score to every reporting user, the treatment of each hazard report's remaining lifespan as a decaying confidence value rather than a fixed timer, and the routing of low-confidence or conflicting reports to a human System Moderator rather than resolving them through automated scoring alone.  
Collective Intelligence Theory, as applied to crowdsourcing and citizen participation, holds that aggregating the dispersed, localized observations of many individual contributors can produce a picture of a situation that is more current and more complete than what a single centralized authority could compile on its own, provided that participation is meaningful, roles are clearly defined, and the resulting information is handled transparently. Mäkipää, Mäenpää, Dang, and Pasanen (2025), in their systematic review of community-driven research for accessibility, found that community-driven approaches are effective precisely because they draw on the direct, first-hand knowledge of individuals who personally encounter the condition being studied, and that this knowledge becomes more reliable and more useful when those individuals are treated as active contributors rather than passive subjects. This theory grounds RouteGuard's foundational premise: that commuters who personally encounter flooding, debris, accidents, or other road-blocking hazards are themselves an important source of localized and timely information about the passability of a given road segment, and that a system built to collect, aggregate, and act on their reports can therefore identify and communicate road hazards more quickly than a system that depends solely on periodic, centralized monitoring.  
Taken together, these two theories position RouteGuard's central design problem as a single, coherent question: how to collect dispersed, commuter-generated observations of road conditions (Collective Intelligence Theory) while establishing enough confidence in any individual report to act on it safely (Trust and Reputation Theory). The Review of Related Literature that follows examines existing studies relevant to both halves of this problem.

**Review of Related Literature**

This section reviews literature relevant to the development of RouteGuard, organized by theme, corresponding to the problems and requirements identified in Chapter I: crowdsourced hazard identification, intelligent rerouting algorithms, low-latency and near-real-time alert mechanisms, trust and reputation systems for verifying user reports, and the detection of non-traffic, physical barriers.

**Local Literature**

**Road Condition Monitoring in the Philippines**

Dacanay, Torio-Kaimo, and Bronuela-Ambrocio (2024), in a paper presented at the 7th International Conference on Civil Engineering (ICOCE 2023\) and published in Springer's Lecture Notes in Civil Engineering, surveyed the road-surveying tools and practices currently used across the Philippines, including onboard vehicle devices, fixed sensors, and audio and video streams, noting that the continued expansion of the national road network under government infrastructure programs makes an inventory-wide monitoring system increasingly necessary. Their assessment shows that formal road monitoring in the country remains oriented toward pavement condition and infrastructure inventory rather than toward real-time, commuter-facing hazard reporting. RouteGuard responds to this gap by complementing formal, periodic monitoring with ongoing crowdsourced hazard reports that can surface road-blocking conditions, such as flooding or debris, as commuters encounter and submit them, rather than waiting for the next scheduled survey.

**Acceptance of Disaster-Oriented Mobile Applications**

Escolano, Caballero, Albina, Hernandez, and Juanatas (2023), presenting at the International Conference on Business and Industrial Research (ICBIR), proposed a smart disaster-management architecture for the Philippines and evaluated user acceptance of a companion mobile application for disaster-preparedness simulation among disaster-management personnel from non-government organizations. Their survey and focus-group results showed high acceptance, with participants rating the application useful and engaging. This finding supports the underlying assumption behind RouteGuard's responder view and its broader mobile-first design: that Filipino disaster-response and community stakeholders are generally receptive to adopting mobile applications as tools for hazard awareness, not merely as consumer conveniences.

Flood Early Warning and Forecasting Systems

Crucillo, Lucero, Gelito, Medina, and Palconit (2026) designed and evaluated an Internet of Things-based Flood Early Warning System (FEWS) for Barangay Doña Imelda, Quezon City, an area repeatedly affected by flooding from the city's river systems. Their system pairs an ESP32 microcontroller with an ultrasonic water-level sensor, a GPS module, and a LoRa radio to transmit water-level readings to a cloud database, which are then displayed through a web dashboard and an Android application to warn residents and local officials. Their barangay-scale, sensor-based approach demonstrates that real-time flood alerting is technically feasible in a Philippine urban setting; RouteGuard applies the same alerting principle, adapted to a near-real-time performance target, to the Tacloban City testing environment without depending on dedicated hardware sensors at every location, instead relying on crowd-sourced reports and municipal advisories to flag a flooded or impassable road as it is encountered.  
Lagmay, Bagtasa, Andal, Andal, Aldea, Bencito, and Liporada (2024), working through the University of the Philippines Resilience Institute's NOAH Center, introduced an impact-based flood forecasting system that follows an anticipatory-action approach, combining calibrated rainfall forecasts with 100-year rainfall return-period data to predict which barangays are likely to flood roughly a day in advance. Where their system is predictive and geared toward pre-event government and community preparedness, RouteGuard is reactive and geared toward the moment a road actually becomes impassable. The two approaches are complementary rather than competing: a day-ahead forecast of this kind could plausibly feed into RouteGuard's Municipal Information Office module as an advance advisory, while RouteGuard's crowd-sourced reporting and rerouting pipeline takes over once flooding is actually observed on the ground.

**Foreign Literature**

**Citizen Involvement in Impact-Based Forecasting**

Sempere-Torres and Berenguer (2024), presenting the concluding synthesis of the European ANYWHERE project in the edited volume Responding to Extreme Weather Events, argue that a genuine shift toward impact-based forecasting, one that predicts what a hazard will do to a community rather than only its physical magnitude, cannot rely on official monitoring and forecasting infrastructure alone. Because vulnerability on the ground changes faster than centralized systems can track, the authors contend that citizen involvement is a structural requirement of impact-based warning, not an optional add-on. This argument reinforces the foundational premise behind RouteGuard: that a centralized municipal advisory system, however well-resourced, cannot alone capture which specific roads are impassable at a given moment, and that a citizen-facing reporting layer is necessary to close that gap between official forecasts and ground-level conditions.

**Task Design in Crowdsourcing Systems**

Wang, Wang, and Zhang (2025), in the Journal of Data, Information and Management, examined how the characteristics of a crowdsourced task, specifically its complexity and ambiguity, affect the quality of the solutions contributors submit, and found that greater interaction between the party seeking the task and the contributor solving it weakens the negative effect that task ambiguity otherwise has on solution quality. Applied to RouteGuard, this finding suggests that the quality of incoming hazard reports depends not only on the reputation system that helps flag them for moderator review after submission, but on how clearly the reporting task itself is framed at the point of entry; an unambiguous, tag-based reporting interface, paired with moderator feedback when a report is flagged, is therefore not just a usability choice but a mechanism supported by the crowdsourcing literature for improving report quality at the source 

**Edge-Based and Real-Time Hazard Detection**

Sahu et al. (2026), in Scientific Reports, proposed a distributed edge-computing framework for real-time hazard detection in smart transportation, combining roadside units, in-vehicle devices, and mobile crowdsensing with ensemble machine-learning models and an alert-distribution layer built on vehicle-to-everything communication, in order to overcome the latency and scalability limits of centralized detection pipelines. Their results, validated through traffic simulation, support the premise underlying RouteGuard's second specific objective: that reported-hazard confirmation and alert delivery must be processed close to the point of need, rather than through a single centralized service, if a system is to recalculate and deliver an alternative route within a few seconds of a hazard being confirmed.  
McMillan, Hill, Moran, Garfein, and Hacker (2025), in Traffic Injury Prevention, conducted a naturalistic study of commercial drivers in California who received in-cab, location-based alerts approximately 500 meters before entering active highway work zones, and found that alerted drivers reduced their speed and generally perceived the alerts as helpful to safer driving. This finding provides direct empirical support for RouteGuard's first specific objective, which likewise sets a 500-meter alerting distance ahead of an eligible hazard: proactive, distance-based warnings of this kind have already been shown, in a real-world commercial driving context, to change driver behavior before a hazard is reached.

**Crowd-Verified Historical Advisory Systems**

Greer et al. (2023), presenting at the International Conference on the Enhanced Safety of Vehicles, proposed CHAMP, a system that advises drivers of likely pedestrian presence by aggregating repeated single-camera detections from a fleet of vehicles into a map of pedestrian hotspots, rather than relying on a single vehicle’s real-time detection at the moment a pedestrian is encountered. Their approach specifically targets the failure cases of conventional detectors, such as darkness and occlusion, by substituting accumulated historical evidence for an in-the-moment sensor reading, and achieved up to 100 percent precision at 75 percent recall in road testing. This crowd-aggregated, history-based approach is conceptually relevant to RouteGuard because, although RouteGuard's reputation score is associated with individual contributors rather than road segments, a location with a consistent history of confirmed hazard reports can still be treated as a standing hotspot even when no single user is currently reporting on it, extending CHAMP’s pedestrian-hotspot logic to the broader class of recurring road hazards, such as chronically flood-prone intersections.

**Trust and Reputation in Crowdsourced Platforms**

Gheyas, Asghar, Schneider, and Woodward (2025), in a systematic review of trust-management practices across crowdsourced platforms, examined Waze's reputation system in detail, describing how contributors earn points and ranks for reporting and confirming hazards while a combination of rule-based logic and machine learning cross-verifies incoming reports. Their review identifies meaningful strengths in this model, such as automated moderation and community validation, but also limitations, including opaque trust metrics, gaps in oversight for smaller or less-active areas, and a tendency for a small group of highly active contributors to dominate map edits. RouteGuard's design directly answers the limitations they identify: rather than relying solely on an automated trust score, RouteGuard routes low-confidence or conflicting reports to a human System Moderator, which is particularly relevant for a localized Tacloban City deployment where the kind of niche oversight gaps Gheyas et al. describe would otherwise be more pronounced.  
Brown, Nadendla, and Das (2024), presenting the Best Paper Award-winning TASR algorithm at IEEE SMARTCOMP 2024, proposed a trust-aware Stackelberg routing framework in which a routing platform accounts for the probability that a given traveler will actually comply with a suggested route, rather than assuming either full compliance or fully selfish behavior. Tested on real road networks, TASR reduced congestion without eroding traveler trust in the platform's recommendations. While RouteGuard's current scope centers on reputation as a measure of report accuracy rather than route compliance, this study points to a natural extension of RouteGuard's reputation system: weighting how strongly an alternative route is pushed to a given user based on that user's own historical trust level, an avenue for future work beyond the present capstone.

**User Preferences for Verification versus Supplementary Information**

Chiang (2023), in a master's thesis completed at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, conducted an online study with 100 participants to test whether people, on encountering inconsistent smart-city sensor readings, would rather use mobile crowdsourcing to verify the information they already have or to obtain additional contextual detail about the situation. The study found that inconsistency did increase people's inclination to seek crowdsourced input, an effect partly explained by reduced trust in sensor accuracy, and that participants leaned slightly toward verification over supplementary context overall, though this preference shifted with perceived urgency, pre-existing expectations, and individual differences. This finding is directly relevant to how RouteGuard's reporting interface should be framed: rather than assuming users always want to add new contextual detail when a route's status looks uncertain, RouteGuard should also support a lightweight, low-effort path for a user to simply confirm or contest an existing report, particularly in urgent situations where speed of response matters more than richness of detail. 

**Crowdsourced Detection of Road-Level Obstacles**

Li, Liu, Xing, Liu, Lin, and Du (2024), in IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems, built a pothole dataset drawn from crowdsourced samples spanning varied road and lighting conditions and used it to train an extended Mask R-CNN model, achieving a mean average precision of 92.1 percent and outperforming standard ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 backbones while also estimating pothole area with low error. Their results demonstrate that crowdsourced image data can support automated, fine-grained classification of a specific class of road hazard. This is directly relevant to RouteGuard's tag-based reporting categories, such as Debris and Partially Passable, and suggests a plausible future enhancement in which photos already attached to a user's report could be automatically pre-classified to assist moderator review, beyond the manual tagging RouteGuard currently relies on.  
Zahura, Goodall, and Chen (2024), in Transportation Research Part D, used crowdsourced Waze traffic data spanning more than four years to quantify the actual travel delays experienced by passenger vehicles during recurrent, tide-driven nuisance flooding in Norfolk, Virginia, comparing vehicle-hours of delay on flooded streets against equivalent dry-day conditions. They found that the most-affected streets saw roughly a 1,500 percent increase in vehicle-hours of delay during flood hours, and that 10 percent of commuters on flooded routes experienced 27 to 73 additional minutes of delay per year during peak periods. This study demonstrates that crowdsourced navigation-app data, of the same general kind RouteGuard collects, can provide useful evidence on its own within the study context, without dedicated flood sensors, to detect and quantify a recurring hazard's real impact on commute times, For RouteGuard, this supports the use of a crowd-reporting layer as a complement to conventional physical infrastructure monitoring, particularly where dedicated sensors are unavailable or limited.  
Yuan, Lee, Mobley, Farahmand, Xu, Blessing, Dong, and Brody (2023), in Computational Urban Science, used crowdsourced Waze reports together with fine-grained traffic data as an indicator of road inundation, combining these with topographic, hydrologic, and rainfall features in random forest and AdaBoost models to predict road flooding risk during Hurricane Harvey and Tropical Storm Imelda in Texas. Their finding that precipitation was the strongest predictor of road inundation, and that crowdsourced reports was found to provide a useful proxy for comparison with available flooding information in that study where sensor coverage was unavailable, reinforces one of RouteGuard's foundational design choices: that reports submitted directly by commuters are a credible signal for identifying a flooded or otherwise impassable road, even in the absence of dedicated flood sensors along every stretch of a route.

**Comparable Multicriteria, Crowdsourcing-Enabled Route Planners**

Fernandes, Dias, and Ferreira (2026), presenting at the Euro Working Group on Transportation Annual Meeting, designed and usability-tested a mobile route-planning application for pedestrians and cyclists that lets users weight routes by safety, comfort, accessibility, and environmental quality, and that incorporates a crowdsourcing module for reporting issues such as damaged sidewalks or poor lighting. Their user survey of 242 respondents found that about 70 percent were willing to contribute reports when the process was quick, and that non-monetary incentives, such as a gamified contributor ranking, were preferred over financial rewards. This is the closest comparable system to RouteGuard in the literature reviewed here: both combine crowdsourced condition reporting with route guidance in a single mobile application. However, their prototype targets active-mobility users choosing among multiple qualitative route criteria and had not yet been integrated with a live routing engine or database at the time of publication, whereas RouteGuard is purpose-built for motorized commuters navigating around road-blocking hazards in near real time, with a dedicated moderation layer and separate channels for municipal advisories and a prototype responder view.  
Taken together, the studies reviewed above show that the individual components of RouteGuard already have independent support in the literature: Philippine research has established both the technical feasibility of localized flood sensing and forecasting and the willingness of Filipino stakeholders to adopt disaster-oriented mobile applications, while international research has validated distance-based proactive alerting, edge-based low-latency hazard detection, crowdsourced flood and pothole detection, and reputation systems for crowdsourced platforms, along with their documented limitations around opaque trust metrics and oversight gaps. Within the literature reviewed here, neither the local nor the foreign body of work presents a single, integrated application that combines near-real-time crowdsourced road-hazard reporting and proximity identification, reputation-informed credibility assessment backed by human moderation, and automatic rerouting into one system purpose-built for urban commuters, while also providing a distinct data channel for official municipal advisories and a prototype responder view for demonstration purposes. This is the gap that RouteGuard is intended to fill.

**Challenges for a Better Use of Crowdsourcing Information**  
Kalas et al. (2024) examined the role of crowdsourced information in enhancing climate emergency situational awareness and early warning systems. The study explored how citizen-generated content, including participatory risk mapping, social media reports, and other forms of crowdsourced data, can supplement traditional disaster risk management (DRM) practices. The authors emphasized that information provided by citizens enables emergency management agencies to obtain real-time, localized, and context-rich data that may not be immediately available through conventional monitoring systems. However, the study also identified several challenges associated with the use of crowdsourced information, including concerns regarding data reliability, misinformation, information overload, inconsistent reporting formats, and the integration of citizen-generated data into existing decision-support systems. To address these issues, the researchers highlighted the importance of implementing validation mechanisms, quality assessment techniques, and intelligent filtering processes to ensure that crowdsourced information remains accurate, relevant, and actionable during emergency situations.  
Its implementation of crowdsourced traffic reporting, the findings of this study are highly relevant to RouteGuard. Similar to the disaster risk management framework presented by Kalas et al. (2024), RouteGuard relies on information contributed by commuters and other road users to provide near-real-time updates regarding road accidents, flooding, road closures, construction-related obstructions, debris, and other road-blocking hazards. These user-generated reports serve as valuable situational awareness data that complement GPS-based navigation and route optimization, enabling the application to recommend safer and more efficient travel routes based on current road conditions rather than static map information.  
Moreover, the study underscores the importance of ensuring the credibility and quality of crowdsourced information before it is utilized for decision-making. This principle directly supports the design of RouteGuard, where user-submitted reports are evaluated using report-confidence and contributor-reputation signals, with final classification performed through human moderation, to prevent inaccurate or misleading information from affecting navigation recommendations. Features such as report confirmation, timestamp information, GPS location matching, contributor reputation scores, and human moderation can improve the trustworthiness of crowdsourced road-hazard data. By incorporating these mechanisms, RouteGuard can reduce the likelihood that unreliable reports are treated as confirmed information while maintaining reliable near-real-time route optimization for its users.  
Another significant contribution of the study is its recognition that citizen participation enhances situational awareness by providing localized information that automated sensing technologies may overlook. Likewise, RouteGuard transforms commuters from passive users into active contributors of transportation intelligence. Instead of relying exclusively on government traffic monitoring systems or roadside sensors, the proposed application supports ongoing collection of community-generated information that reflects actual road conditions as they occur. This collaborative approach allows the system to respond more rapidly to unexpected incidents and improves its ability to identify optimal travel routes in dynamic urban environments.

**Temporal Decay in Crowdsourced Trust Systems**  
Beyond the reputation-system literature already discussed, industry-scale crowdsourced navigation platforms offer additional evidence that report lifespan should not be treated as a fixed duration. According to Waze’s official help documentation, a hazard report remains visible on the map for a length of time that adjusts dynamically based on how other users respond to it: continued confirmation from nearby users extends the report’s display time, while a user marking the hazard as no longer present shortens it (Waze, n.d.). This confirms that an incremental and decremental approach to report lifespan is not merely a theoretical alternative to a fixed timer, but a design pattern already validated at production scale in a widely used navigation application.  
This pattern is further supported by research on temporal reputation modeling in crowdsourcing systems. Kanaparthy, Damle, and Gujar (2021) proposed a reputation framework in which a contributor’s trust score is not static but evolves over time, rising gradually with sustained positive contributions while dropping sharply in response to negative signals, an asymmetry intended to reward consistency while still allowing the system to respond quickly to unreliable behavior. Applied to RouteGuard, this principle supports treating each hazard report’s remaining lifespan as a dynamic confidence score rather than a fixed countdown: the score decays naturally at a rate tied to the hazard category, is extended when other users confirm the report, and is reduced sharply when users indicate the hazard is no longer present, weighted according to the reporting and confirming users’ own reputation scores. When a report’s confidence falls below a set floor without a clear consensus between confirmations and denials, it is escalated to the moderation queue rather than removed outright, integrating this mechanism directly into RouteGuard’s existing verification workflow rather than introducing a separate, disconnected system.

**Community-Driven Research and Crowdsourcing for Accessibility**  
Mäkipää, Mäenpää, Dang, and Pasanen (2025) conducted a systematic review examining how participants are integrated into community-driven research for accessibility. The study explored the application of citizen science and crowdsourcing in addressing accessibility-related challenges across various domains, including transportation, environmental accessibility, and public infrastructure. The researchers found that community-driven approaches are effective because they leverage the knowledge and experiences of individuals who directly encounter accessibility issues in their daily lives. Participants contributed in different capacities, such as data collectors, information providers, and active collaborators in solving accessibility problems. The review also emphasized that meaningful user participation, transparency, trust, and clearly defined participant roles are essential factors for the success of crowdsourced systems. Furthermore, the authors noted that accessibility solutions become more reliable and user-centered when the intended beneficiaries actively contribute to data collection and decision-making processes.  
The study’s implementation of crowdsourced reporting and collaborative navigation provides a strong theoretical foundation for RouteGuard. Similar to the community-driven approach discussed by Mäkipää et al. (2025), RouteGuard depends on active participation from commuters, motorists, cyclists, and pedestrians to collect near-real-time information regarding road accidents, flooding, construction-related obstructions, road closures, and other road-blocking hazards. Rather than relying solely on government traffic monitoring systems or static mapping services, RouteGuard empowers its users to become contributors of valuable transportation data, enabling the application to generate more accurate and timely route recommendations.  
Moreover, the systematic review highlights that involving end users directly in information gathering improves both the quality and relevance of the data collected. This principle aligns closely with RouteGuard's collaborative design, where navigation accuracy is continuously enhanced through user-generated reports that complement GPS location tracking and route optimization algorithms. The study also underscores the importance of user trust, participation incentives, and transparent handling of crowdsourced information, all of which are critical considerations in the development of RouteGuard. Incorporating mechanisms such as report verification, contributor reputation, and ongoing report validation can improve the credibility of submitted information while minimizing inaccurate or misleading reports.  
Additionally, the review demonstrates that crowdsourcing extends beyond simple data collection by fostering community engagement in solving real-world accessibility and mobility challenges. Likewise, RouteGuard transforms its users from passive consumers of navigation services into active participants in improving urban mobility. As more users contribute road-condition information, the application can better identify suitable routes and respond to changing road conditions; predictive travel-delay modeling remains outside the current project scope. This collaborative intelligence enhances the effectiveness of near-real-time route optimization while promoting safer, more efficient, and more accessible urban transportation.

**NaviNote: Enabling In-situ Spatial Annotation Authoring to Support Exploration and Navigation**  
Chen et al. (2026) developed NaviNote, an accessible navigation system designed to support blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals through high-precision localization and collaborative spatial annotations. The study addressed the limitations of conventional GPS navigation, particularly in "last-few-meters" scenarios where location accuracy often degrades. To overcome this challenge, the researchers integrated a Visual Positioning System (VPS), voice-based interaction, conversational artificial intelligence, and user-generated spatial annotations into a single navigation platform. Through user studies involving 24 participants during the design phase and 18 participants during system evaluation, the researchers found that NaviNote significantly improved navigation performance, environmental awareness, and users' ability to create and access location-specific annotations. The study further demonstrated that collaborative spatial annotations enrich navigation by providing contextual information beyond what traditional maps or GPS services can deliver.  
The findings of this study are highly relevant to RouteGuard, particularly regarding the use of collaborative, location-based information to enhance navigation accuracy. Similar to NaviNote, RouteGuard recognizes that navigation is more effective when users can access near-real-time contextual information generated by other members of the community. While NaviNote focuses on accessibility for blind and low-vision users through precise spatial annotations and voice interaction, RouteGuard applies the same collaborative principle to urban transportation by allowing commuters to report road accidents, flooding, construction-related obstructions, road closures, and other road-blocking hazards. These user-generated reports provide contextual information that traditional navigation applications may not immediately detect, enabling more responsive and adaptive route recommendations.  
Furthermore, NaviNote demonstrates the value of integrating user participation into navigation systems rather than relying exclusively on automated positioning technologies. This concept supports RouteGuard's crowdsourcing mechanism, where commuters actively contribute near-real-time information that updates the application's hazard and routing data as reports are submitted and processed. As additional reports are submitted and verified, the system becomes increasingly capable of identifying optimal travel paths while avoiding hazards and delays. The study also highlights the importance of intuitive interaction, accurate localization, and reliable information management, which are essential design considerations for RouteGuard to ensure that crowdsourced reports remain trustworthy, relevant, and beneficial to all users.  
Another important contribution of the study is its emphasis on combining advanced positioning technologies with collaborative intelligence. Although RouteGuard does not require specialized Visual Positioning Systems like NaviNote, the research reinforces the value of integrating GPS-based location tracking with user-generated spatial information to improve navigation performance. By leveraging smartphones, GPS services, and crowdsourced incident reporting, RouteGuard extends this concept to a broader urban environment where route optimization depends not only on geographic location but also on continuously changing road conditions and community-generated hazard reports.  
**Conceptual Framework**

![][image1]

Figure 2-1. Conceptual Framework of RouteGuard (Input-Process-Output Model with Moderation Feedback Loop)

The conceptual framework of this study follows an Input-Process-Output (IPO) model. The input consists of raw data drawn from multiple sources: user-submitted hazard reports, official advisory entries representing the Municipal Information Office, GPS/location data from the reporting user’s device, OpenStreetMap road-network data, and reputation/history data associated with reporting users. The process stage covers the core functions of RouteGuard: report-confidence calculation for incoming reports, automated reputation scoring of reporting users, a moderation queue in which authorized moderators review reports flagged as low-trust, conflicting, or suspicious and resolve reported-hazard confirmation, proximity checking within a 5-kilometer radius of a given user, and route computation and alternative-route generation through OSRM whenever a hazard is confirmed along a commuter’s path. The output consists of the user-facing results of this process: near-real-time push notifications and a recalculated route delivered to the commuter, confirmed hazards displayed on the mobile map, a prototype responder display for demonstration purposes, an advisory status view for MIO personnel, and moderation outcomes recorded for each resolved report. A feedback loop closes the framework: each moderator resolution, confirmed, false, or inconclusive, is fed back into the reporting user’s reputation score, so that the outcome of human review updates the reporting user’s reputation score and influences subsequent report-confidence calculations.

**Definition of Terms**

**Crowd-sourcing.** Conceptually, the practice of obtaining data or input by soliciting contributions from a large group of people, typically via an online platform, rather than from traditional employees or suppliers. Operationally, the process by which RouteGuard collects hazard reports directly from its user base rather than from a single centralized data source.

**Intelligent Routing Algorithm.** Conceptually, a set of computational rules or procedures used to determine an efficient path between two points based on dynamic conditions. Operationally, the software logic within RouteGuard responsible for computing an alternative path once a reported road-blocking hazard has been confirmed along a commuter's original route, targeted to complete within three seconds under typical network conditions.

**Moderation Queue.** Conceptually, a review workflow, common to crowdsourced and social platforms, in which flagged user-generated content is routed to an authorized human reviewer before it is treated as fully trusted. Operationally, the interface within RouteGuard's administrative dashboard through which an authorized moderator reviews hazard reports flagged as low-trust, conflicting, or suspicious, and resolves each as confirmed, false, or inconclusive.

**Municipal Information Office (MIO) Dashboard.** Conceptually, a web-based administrative interface through which a local government office manages and disseminates official public information. Operationally, the standalone web module developed in this study that allows authorized municipal personnel to post, edit, and remove official road advisories for display within the RouteGuard mobile application.

**Preset Hazard Tag.** Conceptually, a predefined, selectable label used in a user interface to categorize input quickly, without requiring free-text entry. Operationally, one of a fixed set of tap-to-select categories (e.g., Flooded, Fully Blocked, Debris, Accident, Partially Passable) that a RouteGuard user selects to submit a hazard report within the 10-second usability target, with free-text description remaining optional.

**Push Notification.** Conceptually, a message delivered directly to a user's mobile device by an application, without the user actively requesting it at that moment. Operationally, the alert RouteGuard sends to a user's device to proactively inform them of a nearby hazard at least 500 meters before they reach it.

**Report Confidence Score.** Conceptually, a numerical indicator of how much certainty can currently be placed in a specific piece of crowdsourced information. Operationally, in this study, the decaying score assigned to an individual hazard report based on its age, the number of confirmations and denials it has received, and the reputation of the contributing users; the score determines a report’s display status and, when it falls below a defined threshold without a clear consensus between confirmations and denials, triggers escalation of the report to the moderation queue rather than automatic confirmation.

| Parameter | Baseline | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| User reputation range | 0–100 | Bounds contributor credibility score |
| First-time reputation | 50 | Neutral baseline before a resolved report outcome |
| Confirmed report update | \+10 | Rewards moderator-confirmed reporting |
| False report update | −15 | Penalizes moderator-classified false reporting |
| Inconclusive update | 0 | No reputation change when evidence is unresolved |
| Confirmation/denial weight | W \= 0.5 \+ (R/100) | Weights evidence by contributor reputation |
| Initial confidence | C0 \= 50 \+ 50 × (Wconfirm − Wdeny)/(Wconfirm \+ Wdeny \+ 1\) | Combines weighted confirmations and denials |
| Decay | C(t) \= max(0, C0 × 2^(−t/H)) | Reduces confidence as hazard information ages |
| Moderation threshold | C(t) \< 40/100 without clear consensus | Escalates low-confidence reports for human review |
| Clear-consensus rule | One side exceeds opposing weighted evidence by ≥20% of total weighted evidence | Prevents automatic escalation when evidence is strongly one-sided |
| Hazard Category | Baseline Confidence Half-Life |  |
| Flooded | 6 hours |  |
| Fully Blocked | 12 hours |  |
| Debris | 12 hours |  |
| Accident | 4 hours |  |
| Partially Passable | 4 hours |  |
| Road Closure | 24 hours |  |

Table 2-2. Baseline Confidence Half-Life by Hazard Category

**Reported-Hazard Proximity Identification.** Conceptually, the process by which a system identifies conditions in the environment that may impede or endanger movement through it. Operationally, in this study, the mechanism by which RouteGuard identifies reported road-blocking hazards within a 5-kilometer radius of a user, filters them for route relevance and confirmation status, and makes eligible confirmed hazards available for notification and rerouting. Geographic proximity alone does not confirm a hazard.

**Reputation Score.** Conceptually, a numerical indicator of a contributor’s historical trustworthiness within a crowdsourced platform. Operationally, in this study, the score assigned to each RouteGuard user based on the outcomes of that user’s previously submitted hazard reports, used to inform report credibility and moderation priority rather than to independently confirm any individual report.

**Reputation System.** Conceptually, a mechanism used in online or crowdsourced platforms to track and score the trustworthiness of a user’s contributions over time. Operationally, the scoring mechanism within RouteGuard that ranks users based on the historical accuracy of their hazard reports; reputation scores inform report credibility and moderation priority but do not themselves confirm a report, as final confirmation of a hazard report remains the responsibility of human moderation review.

**Responder View.** Conceptually, a role-specific interface within a system, tailored to the operational needs of a particular class of user. Operationally, the prototype view within the RouteGuard mobile application that demonstrates how confirmed, active hazard reports could be presented to accredited rescue and emergency response personnel; it is not operationally integrated with an actual agency.

**Route Optimization.** Conceptually, the process of selecting, among available paths, the one that best satisfies a given set of criteria such as distance, time, or safety. Operationally, in this study, the process by which RouteGuard selects an alternative path that avoids a confirmed road-blocking hazard while remaining efficient for the commuter.

**Project Development Cost**

This section itemizes the one-time development-phase costs (capital expenditures, or CAPEX) incurred in building and preparing RouteGuard for pilot deployment. Ongoing operational expenditures (OPEX) such as recurring cloud hosting, post-launch maintenance, or marketing — are excluded from this table, consistent with the distinction between development cost and operating cost. As discussed under Materials, RouteGuard’s backend, database, cache, and routing engine are hosted on a free-tier cloud instance during development and pilot evaluation, so no recurring hosting expenditure is capitalized here; this choice is revisited under the cost-benefit discussion below.

**Cost Justification and Estimation Methodology**

Application distribution for testing is valued at ₱0.00 because sideloading and Firebase App Distribution require no paid developer account, unlike a Google Play Store listing, which is unnecessary until an eventual public production launch outside this capstone’s scope. The domain/hostname item is likewise valued at ₱0.00 because, for the development and pilot-testing phase this study covers, a free subdomain from a dynamic-DNS provider is sufficient to reach the administrative dashboard and API endpoint; a paid, registered domain is not required until a future production launch beyond this capstone’s scope. The backend, database, and mobile development tools listed — Node.js, Express.js, PostgreSQL, PostGIS, Valkey, OSRM, OpenStreetMap data, Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, React, Git/GitHub, Postman, and Figma — are likewise valued at ₱0.00 for the development period because they are available under their respective free or open-source licenses (e.g., MIT, Apache-2.0, and the Open Data Commons Open Database License for OpenStreetMap data). This is distinct from an academic waiver of a tool that is normally sold commercially; no such waived-license tool was used in this project, so no nominal capitalized value is assigned to that line. This table does not include a capitalized cost for developer labor: because the proponents are the system’s own developers completing this project as a degree requirement rather than an externally paid development team, no imputed labor cost is assigned here, and the table instead reflects only the actual, out-of-pocket resources acquired or utilized during development.

**Capitalization as an Organizational Asset**

Upon completion, the RouteGuard codebase — comprising the backend API, the PostgreSQL/PostGIS database schema, the Android application, and the administrative dashboard — is capitalized as an Intangible Asset, since it constitutes custom-developed software and database design rather than physical equipment. This project has no Tangible Asset (Property, Plant, and Equipment) component: no dedicated physical hardware was acquired, as development relies on the proponents’ own existing computers and Android devices, and the backend is deployed on a free-tier cloud instance rather than purchased server hardware. It is worth noting that the capitalized figure in Table 3-3 (₱0.00) reflects only third-party, out-of-pocket costs — all of which were free-tier or open-source resources — and does not monetize the proponents’ own development effort; the system’s functional and technical value as a working asset therefore substantially exceeds its capitalized cost, a common characteristic of student-developed software where both tooling and labor are contributed rather than purchased. The capitalized amount is assumed to amortize on a straight-line basis over a three-year useful life, as an assumption used for this project's projection, with residual value assumed to be zero given the pace of technological change in mobile platforms and mapping data standards.

**Cost-Benefit Analysis and Future Projections**

The total development cost of ₱0.00 compares favorably against the recurring cost of the present, manual system described earlier in this chapter, under which Tacloban City commuters and LGU personnel rely on disconnected social media posts, radio announcements, and barangay-level notices to disseminate hazard information. That present approach carries an ongoing, largely uncounted cost in LGU staff time spent manually cross-posting advisories across multiple channels, and in commuter time and safety risk lost to delayed or missed hazard information. RouteGuard’s minimal one-time development cost, by contrast, capitalizes a reusable system rather than an ongoing manual process, and because both hosting and the domain/hostname are free-tier during this evaluation phase, the marginal operating cost beyond the initial already-minimal capitalization is effectively zero. Should the Tacloban City LGU formally adopt RouteGuard beyond the pilot phase, the primary future cost would be a modest, predictable recurring hosting and domain expenditure (see Materials) rather than a repeat of the one-time development investment, giving the system a clear pathway toward a positive return on investment as adoption grows.

**Data**

**Systems Environment**

**Population of the Study**

The population of this study consists of two respondent groups relevant to the evaluation of RouteGuard: (a) commuters residing in or regularly traveling through Tacloban City, Leyte, who represent the application’s primary end users, and (b) authorized administrative personnel from the Tacloban City local government unit (LGU) who represent the intended users of the administrative dashboard and moderation functions. Given the impracticality of surveying the entire commuting population of the city, this study uses purposive sampling with separate eligibility criteria for each respondent group. Commuter respondents are eligible if they are Tacloban City residents or regular travelers who regularly use roads potentially affected by road-blocking hazards, giving them direct, relevant experience with the problem RouteGuard addresses. Administrative respondents are eligible if they are authorized personnel representing the Municipal Information Office (MIO) or moderation functions and are able to evaluate the administrative dashboard and moderation features. A target of at least 30 commuter respondents and 5 authorized administrative respondents is set for the planned pilot user-acceptance and system-evaluation activities of this capstone. The five administrative respondents represent the MIO and moderation functions included in the prototype evaluation. Because these respondents are selected based on their relevance to the prototype's administrative functions, administrative results are interpreted as role-specific descriptive feedback and are not generalized to the entire LGU workforce.

**Description of the Present System**

At present, commuters in Tacloban City rely on a combination of general-purpose navigation applications, such as Waze and Google Maps, and informal, disconnected channels to stay informed of road hazards and advisories. General-purpose navigation applications provide routing and, in Waze’s case, community-reported incidents, but these reports are not tailored to the hazard categories most relevant to a flood-prone Philippine city, such as flooding, debris, or partial road blockage, and depend on a global user base whose local reporting density in Tacloban City is inconsistent. Official hazard and road-advisory information, when available, is typically disseminated separately through LGU social media pages, local radio announcements, or barangay-level notices, none of which are integrated into any navigation platform a commuter might already be using while traveling. As a result, a commuter must actively monitor multiple, unconnected sources, often only after already encountering a hazard, rather than being proactively alerted to it while en route.

**Limitations/Drawbacks of the Present System**

This fragmented approach has several drawbacks that directly motivate this study, consistent with the gaps identified in Chapter I. First, information reaches commuters with significant delay, since official advisories are posted independently of a commuter’s live location and general navigation applications are not tuned to local reporting patterns. Second, general-purpose navigation platforms do not provide the project's full set of locally defined road-blocking hazard categories, and do not treat flooding, debris, or partial road blockage as first-class, taggable hazard categories. Third, community-submitted reports on general-purpose platforms are not independently verified through any moderation process, leaving commuters with no reliable way to judge how much confidence to place in a given report. Finally, because official advisories and crowd-sourced reports reside on separate platforms, a commuter has no single, unified information source that combines both — a gap RouteGuard is designed to close.

**Methods**

**Research Design and Evaluation Approach**  
For this capstone proposal, a developmental-evaluative research design is used: Agile Scrum guides system development, while the completed prototype is evaluated through technical testing together with user-acceptance evaluation. Agile Scrum is treated as the development methodology, not as the research design.

**System Development Life Cycle**

This study adopts the Agile Scrum framework as its system development methodology. The research evaluation is conducted through technical testing and user-acceptance evaluation described in the Evaluation section. RouteGuard’s core subsystems — reported-hazard proximity identification and alerting, route optimization, tag-based reporting, the reputation and report-confidence mechanism, and the moderation module — are interdependent but individually testable. The report-confidence parameters defined in this proposal serve as the baseline configuration for implementation and testing; if prototype evidence requires refinement, any changed parameter must be documented, justified, and re-tested rather than altered informally. Scrum’s iterative sprint structure allows each subsystem to be developed, demonstrated, and adjusted incrementally while preserving the study’s defined objectives and measurable baseline requirements.  
The development team assumes the roles typical of a small Scrum team: the proponents serve as the Development Team, the project adviser serves as the Product Owner responsible for validating each increment against the study’s specific objectives, and one proponent rotates as Scrum Master to facilitate sprint ceremonies. Each sprint follows a two-week cycle consisting of sprint planning, daily stand-ups, a sprint review with the adviser, and a sprint retrospective. The product backlog is derived directly from the study objectives, scope, and system specifications defined in Chapter I. **Procedures for the Different Phases**

Development proceeds across seven sprints, each corresponding to a discrete increment of the system. Figure 3-2 shows the context-level data flow supporting these procedures, tracing the principal system interactions of the Commuter/Reporting User, authorized MIO personnel, and System Moderator; the prototype Responder View is not included in the formal respondent evaluation.

![][image3]

Figure 3-2. Context-Level (Level 0\) Data Flow Diagram of RouteGuard

* Sprint 0 – Project Setup and Environment Preparation. Establish the development environment, initialize the backend and mobile repositories, configure the PostgreSQL schema, provision the self-hosted OSRM engine with an OpenStreetMap extract of Tacloban City, Leyte, and set up the Valkey instance.

* Sprint 1 – Core Map and Reported-Hazard Proximity Identification (SO1). Develop the mobile map interface, implement geofencing logic to identify reported hazards within a 5-kilometer radius of the user, and implement the push notification system that alerts users at least 500 meters before reaching an eligible confirmed, route-relevant hazard.

* Sprint 2 – Route Optimization (SO2). Integrate the mobile client and backend with the self-hosted OSRM engine using the Multi-Level Dijkstra (MLD) algorithm, and implement automatic rerouting targeting a 3-second response time from confirmation of a reported road-blocking hazard.

* Sprint 3 – Reporting, Reputation, and Report Confidence (SO3). Build the tag-based hazard-reporting interface with a sub-10-second submission target, implement the user reputation-scoring system, and implement the report-confidence decay mechanism, including per-category confidence half-lives and confirmation/denial weighting.

* Sprint 4 – Administrative Dashboard and Advisories (SO4). Develop the web-based administrative dashboard that allows authorized municipal personnel to post, edit, and remove official road advisories, ensuring newly posted advisories propagate to the mobile hazard map within 5 seconds.

* Sprint 5 – Moderation Module (SO5). Implement the moderation queue within the administrative dashboard, enabling authorized moderators to review flagged and conflicting hazard reports and resolve each as confirmed, false, or inconclusive.

* Sprint 6 – System Integration, Testing, and Refinement. Conduct integration testing across all subsystems, execute user acceptance testing with the respondents described under Population of the Study, and refine the system based on evaluation results prior to final defense.

**Evaluation**

RouteGuard is evaluated using the ISO/IEC 25010 software product quality model, applied separately to the commuter-facing and administrative-facing components of the system. Given the scope of this study, evaluation focuses on five quality areas aligned with ISO/IEC 25010 and most directly tied to the specific objectives defined in Chapter I: Feature Completeness and Correctness (whether reported-hazard proximity identification, routing, reporting, and moderation perform their intended functions completely and correctly), Performance Efficiency (whether the 3-second reroute and 5-second advisory-propagation targets are met under typical network conditions), Reliability (whether the system maintains correct report-confidence and reputation state throughout scheduled test sessions), Usability (whether the tag-based reporting interface can be completed in under 10 seconds by an average user), and Security (whether user accounts, reputation data, and moderation actions are protected against unauthorized access or manipulation). Not every characteristic applies equally to both respondent groups: commuter respondents rate items concerning reporting, notifications, the hazard map, route optimization, and usability, while administrative respondents rate items concerning the dashboard, moderation, advisories, and other administrative functions.  
A structured questionnaire, adapted from the ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics above, is administered separately to the commuter respondents and to the administrative respondents identified under Population of the Study following user acceptance testing, with item content tailored to the features each group evaluates. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale (5 – Strongly Agree, 4 – Agree, 3 – Neutral, 2 – Disagree, 1 – Strongly Disagree).  
In addition to the questionnaire, objective technical tests are used for the performance and verification-related targets. Verification testing uses a predefined baseline test matrix of 30 reports: 12 true/confirmable cases, 8 false-report cases, 5 conflicting-report cases, and 5 inconclusive cases, with expected outcomes established before execution. Each conflicting case is assigned a predefined expected outcome before testing based on its prescribed evidence and moderation scenario. Each case is processed by the system and compared with its expected classification; verification accuracy is computed from exact correct classifications, while false-positive cases are recorded separately. The test matrix includes different hazard categories and confidence conditions so that the report-confidence and moderation logic are exercised rather than tested only under one scenario. Route-recalculation time, advisory propagation time, reporting completion time, notification delivery time, and concurrent-request behavior are measured from system test runs and recorded as technical results rather than inferred from respondent perception. Role-based access is checked using predefined authorization test cases for ordinary users, MIO personnel, and System Moderators.

| Test Case Group | Number of Cases | Expected Outcome |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| True/confirmable | 12 | Confirmed |
| False-report | 8 | False |
| Conflicting-report | 5 | Predefined per test scenario before execution |
| Inconclusive | 5 | Inconclusive |

For the technical verification tests, verification accuracy is computed as the number of test reports whose final system classification exactly matches the predefined expected classification divided by the total number of test reports, multiplied by 100\. An expected inconclusive case is counted as correct only when the system returns inconclusive; an expected confirmed case is counted as correct only when the system returns confirmed; and an expected false case is counted as correct only when the system returns false. A false positive is defined as a negative test case (expected false or otherwise not confirmed) that the system classifies as confirmed. The false-positive rate is calculated as FPR \= (FP / N) × 100, where FP is the number of false positives and N is the total number of predefined negative test cases in the relevant test set. False-positive counts and rates are reported for each relevant test set.  
Responses are summarized using the weighted mean, computed separately for the commuter evaluation and the administrative evaluation, for each ISO/IEC 25010 characteristic as WM \= Σ(fw) / N, where f is the number of respondents selecting a given scale point, w is the numerical weight of that scale point (1 through 5), and N is the actual number of valid respondents in the relevant group. The target minimums are 30 commuter respondents and 5 administrative respondents; if more valid responses are collected, all valid responses are included in N. The weighted means of the two groups are reported and interpreted separately and are not combined into a single pooled score. The resulting weighted mean for each characteristic, and for each instrument overall, is interpreted using the following scale: 4.20–5.00 as Excellent, 3.40–4.19 as Very Satisfactory, 2.60–3.39 as Satisfactory, 1.80–2.59 as Fair, and 1.00–1.79 as Poor.
